book: Chapter 19 · Choosing the Appropriate Architecture Style
title: It Depends, With a Method
gist: The chapter that refuses to answer the question — and then gives you the seven things to know first, the three decisions to make in order, and two worked designs that show what the answer looks like.
minute: Architecture fashion shifts for reasons: **observations from past pain**, ecosystem change, new capabilities, acceleration, domain change, technology change, and external factors like licence cost.

Seven things to know before choosing: the **domain**, the **architecture characteristics**, the **data architecture**, **cloud deployment**, **organisational factors**, **process/teams/operations**, and **domain-architecture isomorphism**.

The star charts throughout Part II rate **characteristics, not domains** — because almost any generic style can implement almost any domain, and the real difference is how well each supports which characteristics.
Three decisions, in order: **monolith or distributed** → **where does data live** → **synchronous or asynchronous**.
**Default to synchronous; go asynchronous only when necessary.** It presents fewer design, implementation and debugging challenges.

sections.t: What you need to know first
sections.alt: Seven decision criteria for choosing an architecture style
sections.cap: Not a checklist to complete — a set of gaps to close before the decision is meaningful.
items: **The domain** — not as a subject-matter expert, but well enough to see what affects operational characteristics. Business analysts fill the gaps.
**Architecture characteristics** — the actual differentiator between styles, which is why every scorecard in Part II is about characteristics rather than domains.
**Data architecture** — a specialisation in its own right, and it matters most when the new system must live alongside an older data design.

**Cloud deployment** — how much data will be stored, and how much has to move (which costs real money). The cloud is also the clearest example of a sophisticated capability becoming a commodity: elasticity used to take esoteric skills and is now a configuration parameter.
**Organisational factors** — a vendor's price can veto the right design. Planned mergers push you toward open solutions and integration architectures.
**Process, teams, operations** — if the organisation lacks maturity in Agile engineering practices, styles that depend on them (microservices) will be painful.

sections.t: Isomorphism: does the shape fit the problem?
sections.alt: Layered against modular monolith shapes, and monolithic against distributed shapes
sections.cap: Figs. 19-1 and 19-2 · *isos* equal, *morph* shape — a map that preserves relations among elements.
sections.p: Some domains match a topology directly. **Microkernel** suits anything needing customisation, because customisations become plug-ins. **Space-based** suits genome analysis, which is a large number of discrete operations. And some domains fit a style badly on purpose: a multipage insurance form where each page depends on the previous one is a **highly semantically coupled problem**, and modelling it in a highly decoupled architecture fights the domain. Service-based — an intentionally coupled architecture — suits it better.

sections.alt: Three sequential questions: monolith or distributed, where data lives, synchronous or asynchronous
sections.sit: You have done the characteristics analysis and the component design. Now the style has to be chosen — and these three questions, taken in order, do most of the choosing.
opts: One set of characteristics suffices → monolithic. Different parts need different sets → distributed. **The architecture quantum from Chapter 7 is the tool** for making this call.

In a monolith, usually one relational database. In a distributed architecture you must decide which services persist what — and that means thinking about how data flows through the workflows, not just where it sits.
Synchronous is more convenient and trades away scalability and reliability. Asynchronous buys performance and scale and hands you data synchronisation, deadlocks, race conditions and debugging.
sections.verdict: **Default to synchronous, and use asynchronous when necessary.** And note what the output of this process actually is: not just a topology, but the topology *plus* the **ADRs** covering the decisions that took the most effort, *plus* the **fitness functions** protecting the principles and operational characteristics you have just committed to.

sections.alt: The Going, Going, Gone microservices design resolved into five quantum boundaries
sections.cap: Fig. 19-6 · GGG resolves to five quanta: Payment, Auctioneer, Bidder, Bidder Streams, Bid Tracker.
items: **Silicon Sandwiches — modular monolith.** One relational database, one web UI designed carefully for mobile, each domain as a component. The style doesn't handle customisation, so that becomes domain design: an **Override endpoint** every domain component references — and a fitness function to check that they do.

**Silicon Sandwiches — microkernel.** Domains and a database in the core; common customisations in one plug-in set, local ones each with their own data. It also uses **Backends for Frontends**: the API layer becomes a thin microkernel adapter, and each BFF (iOS, Android, web) reshapes generic backend output — format, pagination, latency — for its device.

**GGG — microservices.** Both event-driven and microservices matched the characteristics; microservices won because it **supports variation in operational characteristics between services**, where pure EDA separates pieces by communication style rather than by characteristics.

The asynchronous choices in GGG exist for a specific reason: Payment processes one payment every 500 ms. If many auctions end at once, synchronous calls become timeouts. **Message queues add reliability to a critical but fragile part of the architecture.**
sections.p: In both cases the separation of tables in the monolith designs is deliberate: partitioning the database along the same lines as the domain components is what makes a later migration to a distributed architecture possible rather than theoretical.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 19: Choosing the Appropriate Architecture Style, pp. 359–370.
